contract_plain_english: If the endpoint-flux balance holds for every spatial interval and q and f(q) are smooth enough for the standard calculus steps, then the integral of q_t + partial_x(f(q)) over every interval is zero. The integrand therefore vanishes pointwise, giving the classical differential conservation law. This conclusion is not asserted at discontinuities.

source_evidence.observation: The identity is required on every interval for arbitrary x1 and x2. Assuming q and f are smooth, the book moves the time derivative inside, represents the endpoint flux difference as an integral of -partial_x f(q), obtains an integral of q_t + partial_x f(q) equal to zero for every interval, and concludes that the integrand is identically zero.

binders: A one-dimensional spatial domain and time variable t.
Arbitrary endpoints x1 < x2 in the spatial domain.
A conserved state q(x,t), scalar or componentwise vector-valued.
An autonomous flux f depending on q.
conclusions: The integrand q_t(x,t) + partial_x(f(q(x,t))) is identically zero.
Hence q satisfies the differential conservation law q_t(x,t) + partial_x(f(q(x,t))) = 0 in the classical pointwise sense.
definitions_and_conventions: The integral of q over [x1,x2] is the total amount of the conserved quantity in that interval, componentwise for a system.
The endpoint sign convention is inflow at x1 minus outflow at x2: f(q(x1,t)) - f(q(x2,t)).
An autonomous flux depends on q but not explicitly on x or t.
The differential form is q_t + partial_x(f(q)) = 0.
hypotheses: For every interval [x1,x2], d/dt integral_[x1,x2] q(x,t) dx = f(q(x1,t)) - f(q(x2,t)).

q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth to differentiate under the integral sign, apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to the flux, and infer pointwise vanishing from vanishing integrals on every interval.
implicit_context: The statement is one-dimensional and homogeneous, with no interior source term.
The derivation is in the smooth classical regime and is explicitly not the framework for shock discontinuities.
The book treats the integral law as the more fundamental conservation statement.

details: The integral identity must hold for every interval, not merely one fixed pair of endpoints.

Sufficient smoothness justifies differentiation under the integral sign and conversion of endpoint fluxes into an integral of a spatial derivative.
The conclusion is a classical pointwise PDE.
